summary:
South Sudan carries a statute that reaches gender presentation on its face: the law criminalises a male person who "dresses or is attired in the fashion of a woman". For a trans visitor presenting female, that provision is the operative exposure, and it does not depend on any sexual conduct or on any disclosure of identity.

The same law treats consensual same-sex sexual conduct as "unnatural offenses", defined as "carnal intercourse against the order of nature", punishable by up to 10 years' imprisonment. Where the conduct is nonconsensual, the term rises to up to 14 years.

United States State Department country reports on human rights practices for 2018, 2019, 2020, 2021 and 2022 each record that there were no reports of authorities enforcing the same-sex conduct provision. The reports describe no repeal, moratorium or prosecutorial policy accompanying that non-enforcement, so the offences remain in force and available to an enforcement authority.

The dress offence is drafted in terms of sex and attire rather than identity or diagnosis. A visitor therefore faces it as a matter of visible presentation, with no threshold of behaviour, documentation or intent to cross first.
tangentialFactors:
The conduct offence and the dress offence are distinct limbs of the law. A trans visitor can be exposed under the second without any exposure under the first, which means advice framed only around sexual conduct understates the statutory position in South Sudan.

Five consecutive annual reports reproduce the same offence wording and the same penalty tiers, which indicates a settled legal position across the 2018 to 2022 reporting period rather than a recent legislative change.

The consistent finding of no reported enforcement sits uneasily with the breadth of the dress offence, and the reports do not explain the gap. Whether that reflects non-prosecution, unrecorded proceedings, or a limitation of the reporting method is unresolved in the current source set.

The penalty structure is asymmetric: the nonconsensual tier carries a longer term than the consensual tier, which means the reports do not treat the provision as operating only against coercive conduct.
localsOnly:
South Sudanese residents live under the same two provisions described above, with the dress offence applying to male persons on the basis of attire in public view.

The State Department reporting for 2018 through 2022 documents no prosecutions, convictions or sentences under either offence, and no official guidance on how the dress provision is applied by police or prosecutors.

Nothing in the current source set records any domestic legal challenge to either provision, any legislative bill to repeal them, or any judicial ruling on their constitutionality.
outOfScopeNotes:
The current source set does not address legal gender recognition, identity-document or passport marker rules, visa and entry screening, airport or border procedures, healthcare access, facilities, hate-crime protection, or recognition of partners. These questions remain unresolved for South Sudan on the present inventory.

The reports identify the offences only by their statutory wording. The name and year of the enacting instrument are not established by this source set, and no claim about a specific Penal Code or enactment year should be read as sourced here.

No source in the inventory documents violence against trans people, community or advocacy organisations, or official statements on gender identity in South Sudan. The absence of such material in this pass is not a finding that no such incidents or organisations exist.

The enforcement finding rests on the reporting method of a single government's annual country reports. Independent monitoring or court-record verification of non-enforcement is not present in the inventory.
